options.misconception: treats only the young as dependent, ignoring older residents

options.misconception: counts all under-65s as dependent, inverting the definition

options.misconception: treats the dependent share as a ratio rather than a fraction

questions.explanation: Dependents are conventionally the under-15s and the 65-and-overs, who are 820 of Halloway's 2,000 residents. That is 41%, and it says nothing about whether older residents actually work.
questions.hint: Add the two age bands, then divide by the total.

questions.topic: Counterfactual design for a transport change
questions.learningObjective: Design a before-and-after comparison that isolates a transport change
questions.stem: I want to know whether the new valley bus cut my own driving to the dark site. Sketch the comparison I should design so that the change in my travel is not confused with other seasonal shifts.

answer.exemplar: Record a pre-change baseline of my journey distances, modes and fuel use over at least eight weeks, then log the same measures for eight weeks after the service starts, keeping the observing nights comparable. Compare per-night distance rather than totals, and note any change in my own habits so a shift in my behaviour is not read as a change in the service.

questions.explanation: A counterfactual needs a before-and-after baseline for the same person, season and task. Keeping observing nights and destinations comparable stops other changes being credited to the bus.
questions.hint: Compare the same route before and after, not two different routes.

questions.stem: The parish is fitting smart meters to test whether the new efficiency advice really cuts the village's electricity use. Explain what would have to be true for the metered results to show a real saving.

answer.exemplar: The saving is only credible if the metered households are representative of the whole village, if the readings cover a comparable season before and after, and if the meter records the same thing on both sides of the change. The same households must be measured on both occasions, and other changes such as a new appliance or a mild spell must be noted, because a one-off change in the weather or in occupancy can masquerade as an efficiency gain.

questions.explanation: Metering shows what happened to the metered homes, not the whole village. The saving generalises only if those homes are typical, the seasons match and no other change is mixed in.
questions.hint: Ask who was measured, when, and what else changed.

questions.stem: I want to publish an estimate of the parish's total household electricity use from the average printed on the energy summary. Describe the check I should run before I trust that number.

answer.exemplar: I should pull the metered or billed totals for a sample of households covering different house sizes and heating types, sum them, and check that the average per household is close to the printed figure. I should also confirm how many households are included, since an average drawn from one tariff or scheme does not describe the whole parish, and record the year the summary covers before scaling it to the full household count.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Counterfactual design for a transport change
questions.learningObjective: Explain why route mileage alone cannot attribute an emissions change
questions.stem: The village has replaced Friday's market bus with a smaller shuttle. Explain why a drop in total car mileage on that route would not by itself show the shuttle caused lower emissions.

answer.exemplar: A fall in mileage on one route can be offset by passengers switching to cars for journeys they used to make on the bus, or by the shuttle running a less direct path with more cold starts and idling. It might also reflect a season with fewer market days, or a competing bus that opened at the same time. To attribute the change to the shuttle I would need the before-and-after journeys of the same passengers, their previous modes and the fuel performance of the replacement vehicle.

questions.explanation: Mileage is an input rather than an outcome, and one route ignores journeys passengers rearrange elsewhere. Mode substitution, route quality and season all move emissions independently of the shuttle.
questions.hint: Ask what passengers did with the journeys they gave up.

answer.exemplar: I would record the weight and date of every collection for a full year, so all seasons and collection frequencies are covered, and I would exclude tonnage from commercial premises that the parish handles but residents do not generate. questions.topic: Totalling a per-household energy average
questions.learningObjective: Explain the limits of scaling a household average to a total
questions.stem: The parish's energy leaflet quotes 2,850 kWh per household per year. Explain why multiplying that by the household count still gives an estimate rather than an exact figure.

answer.exemplar: The average hides the spread. Some households heat with oil or wood and use far more than 2,850 kWh, while flats with electric cooking and no immersion heater use much less, so the true total depends on the mix of homes and how representative the quoted average is of that mix. The count also has to cover the same year and the same definition of household, and any household that moved in or out during the year is only partly counted. The result is a good central estimate, not a measurement.

questions.explanation: The average stands in for a spread of households rather than describing them, so multiplying it by a count gives a good estimate only if it is representative. Household definitions and mid-year moves add further uncertainty.
questions.hint: An average says nothing about how homes differ.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why cost per passenger misleads across differently shaped networks
questions.stem: The bus company's route map covers four villages. Explain why a single cost per passenger figure can mislead readers about the villages it serves.

answer.exemplar: A single figure hides which village carries which cost. Fixed costs such as the depot, the timetable and the vehicles are spread over whoever is carried on each run, so a village with a long thin route that attracts few passengers pays a high cost per head, while a compact village on a busy corridor can look cheap per passenger. The cost per passenger also falls as more people board the same bus, so it moves with demand rather than describing the service. Readers need the cost allocated per village, with fixed and variable parts separated.

questions.explanation: Cost per passenger mixes fixed costs, which do not shrink with ridership, with variable ones, so it moves with demand and is not comparable between differently shaped villages. Allocating fixed costs to the villages that trigger them makes the comparison fair.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the combined effect of per-person change and population growth on a total
questions.stem: Halloway's residents cut their waste per person by 8 per cent last year while the population grew 5 per cent. Explain what that means for the total the tip received.

answer.exemplar: The two changes pull in opposite directions, so the total is close to unchanged rather than clearly lower. Per-resident use is 0.92 times its old level and the population is 1.05 times, so total volume is 0.92 times 1.05, which is 0.966, about 3.4 per cent below the previous year. The community's effort has largely been absorbed by the extra residents, and the trend would reverse if population growth continued at that pace.

questions.topic: Index form of an emissions identity
questions.learningObjective: Explain the interpretive value of the index form of the identity
questions.stem: Explain what the index form of an emissions identity tells you that a simple total does not.

answer.exemplar: A total says how much is emitted and nothing about why, so it cannot tell a village whether to change its population, how active each person is, or how much service the village provides. The index splits the total into population, activity per person and service output, and by expressing each as a ratio to a base year it shows which factor moved. That matters because the three factors point to different decisions, and fixing two of them shows how much of any change comes from the third.

questions.explanation: The identity breaks a total into population, activity per person and service output, each as a ratio to a base year. That shows which factor moved, so you know where the change came from and which lever to pull.
questions.hint: Ask which of the three factors changed.

questions.topic: Allowances against tradable caps
questions.learningObjective: Explain how allowance trading distributes the burden of a cap
questions.stem: Explain why tradable allowances can hold a total emissions cap while individual firms change their behaviour in very different ways.

answer.exemplar: The cap fixes the total, but the allowances decide who is allowed to emit, and firms respond to the allowance price rather than to the cap itself. A firm that has cut its costs easily will sell spare allowances and benefit from trading, while a firm facing high compliance costs will hold on and pay instead. Firms that need allowances badly may end up with no cash left to invest in cleaner equipment, so the same cap can tighten a sector's output or shift emissions abroad, depending on who holds the allowances.

questions.explanation: Trading equalises the cost of the last tonne, so behaviour depends on each firm's abatement options and cash. A firm with cheap options sells allowances and invests, while a cash-poor firm may buy compliance without cutting output.
questions.hint: Firms respond to the allowance price, not the cap.

questions.topic: Per-resident waste from a municipal record
questions.learningObjective: Calculate per-resident weekly waste from a four-week collection record
questions.stem: Parish collection slips record 12.0, 13.5, 11.5 and 13.0 tonnes of refuse over four weeks, and Halloway has 5,000 residents. What is waste per resident per week in kilograms?
questions.explanation: The four weeks total 50 tonnes, which is 50,000 kg, and 50,000 over 5,000 residents is 10 kg each per week. Averaging the weekly weights first gives a typical week's 12.5 tonnes, not the four-week total.
questions.hint: Sum the four weeks before dividing by residents.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Totalling a per-household energy average
questions.learningObjective: Scale a leaflet average and note the coverage limits of its source

stimulus.body: A parish energy leaflet states that the average household in Halloway uses 2,850 kWh of electricity a year and that the parish contains 1,240 households. A footnote says the average comes from supplier billing data covering the year to March.

questions.stem: Using the leaflet, what total annual household electricity use does the parish use, and what should a reader remember about it?

options.text: Exactly 3,534,000 kWh, since every household is included in the billing data used.
options.misconception: treats a billing average as an exact measurement of every home

options.text: 2,850 kWh a year for the parish as a whole, because the leaflet gives a parish figure.
options.misconception: reads a per-household figure as a parish-wide total

options.text: About 3,534,000 kWh, an estimate that assumes the billed average represents every home.
3,534,000 kWh a year, but only for the year ending March rather than a calendar year.
options.misconception: treats the coverage note as if it changed the arithmetic

questions.explanation: Scaling the average by the household count gives 2,850 × 1,240 = 3,534,000 kWh. The footnote matters: the average comes from billing data for a year ending in March, so the total is an estimate for a non-calendar period.
questions.hint: Scale the average, then note the period the average covers.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Counterfactual design for a transport change
questions.learningObjective: Interpret before-and-after journey means without overreaching
questions.stem: Before the valley bus I logged 40 journeys averaging 14.0 km; after it started I logged 40 averaging 11.2 km. What does the pair of means support?

options.text: Total driving fell by 20 per cent, since the same number of journeys was logged.
options.misconception: assumes equal journey counts transfer the percentage to totals

options.text: Nothing can be concluded, because 40 journeys is too few to say anything.
options.misconception: dismisses a moderate sample as unusable for any conclusion

options.text: Fuel use fell by 20 per cent, because distance and fuel move together.
options.misconception: treats shorter journeys as automatically meaning less fuel

options.text: Mean journey distance fell by 20 per cent, though mode and occupancy still need checking.

questions.explanation: The mean distance change is 2.8 km on 14.0 km, which is 20 per cent. Distance is not fuel: vehicles used, idling and occupancy all matter, so this supports a travel-pattern change, not a quantified saving.
questions.hint: Distance changed; emissions need more than distance.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Metered checks for an efficiency programme
questions.learningObjective: Design a control-group trial of a household efficiency programme
questions.stem: The parish wants evidence that its efficiency programme cuts household electricity use rather than shifting it. Describe the trial design you would run.

answer.exemplar: I would recruit two comparable groups of households from the same streets, meter both for a full year and record the before and after readings for each home, and install the programme in one group while the other waits a year. I would record appliance changes, heating fuel switches and occupancy in both groups, because those are the things that move electricity use without any efficiency gain. I would analyse the difference in change between the groups rather than the after-levels alone, and publish the group sizes so readers can see how confident the result is.

questions.explanation: A waiting control group turns the trial into a comparison of changes, removing the effect of a mild winter or a busy season. Recording what households do anyway, such as new appliances, reveals a shift in use rather than a saving.
questions.hint: Use a waiting group and compare changes, not after-levels.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Total against per-person footprint for a city
questions.learningObjective: Explain how falling per-person emissions coexist with a rising total
questions.stem: Explain why the same city can show a falling per-person emissions footprint and a rising total in the same year.

answer.exemplar: The two figures answer different questions because the total grows with population while the per-person figure strips population out. A city with 200,000 residents emitting 1,600,000 tonnes has a footprint of 8 tonnes each; if population rises 5 per cent to 210,000 while the footprint falls to 7.8 tonnes each, the total becomes 1,638,000 tonnes, which is higher than before. The per-person fall is real and useful, but it does not reduce the total unless it outweighs the extra residents.

questions.explanation: A total is population times a per-person rate, so a falling rate can sit with a rising total whenever growth is large enough. Both matter: the per-person figure tracks efficiency, the total tracks scale of impact.
questions.hint: The two numbers use different denominators.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Allowances against tradable caps
questions.learningObjective: State precisely what an emissions cap controls
questions.stem: A trading scheme issues one allowance per tonne of emissions and caps the total. Which statement best describes what the cap actually controls?

options.text: The emissions of each firm, because every firm must hold an allowance for each tonne.
options.misconception: confuses a firm-level holding with a firm-level obligation

options.text: The price of allowances, which the regulator sets directly from the cap.
options.misconception: believes the regulator fixes the allowance price

options.text: The technology firms use, since allowances oblige them to invest in new equipment.
options.misconception: assumes allowances dictate firms' technology choices

options.text: The total emissions of the capped sector, because allowances issued equal the cap.

questions.explanation: The cap fixes the number of allowances and so the maximum tonnes the covered sector may emit. The allowance price comes from trading, and firms choose their own abatement, so the cap binds the total rather than any one firm.
questions.hint: The cap limits tonnes in total, not tonnes per firm.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Population growth against per-person consumption
questions.learningObjective: Compute total consumption after population and per-resident changes
questions.stem: Halloway's population rose from 4,000 to 4,400 residents, and weekly consumption per resident fell from 12.0 kg to 11.5 kg. What is the town's total weekly consumption now, in kilograms?
questions.explanation: The new total is the new population times the new rate per person: 4,400 × 11.5 kg = 50,600 kg a week. Before the change it was 4,000 × 12.0 = 48,000 kg, so more people outweighed the lower rate.
questions.hint: Multiply the new population by the new per-resident figure.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Network cost per person in compact form
questions.learningObjective: Infer the effect of a fixed network charge on cost per resident

stimulus.body: The water utility's account shows an annual network cost of 320,000 for the area, a customer base of 4,000 residents, and a note that the figure includes a fixed reservoir charge that does not change with the number of customers.

questions.stem: Using the account, what does the fixed reservoir charge inside the annual cost imply for the network's cost per resident?

options.text: It is 320,000 each, since a fixed charge is not affected by the number of residents.
options.misconception: treats a fixed total charge as a per-person amount

options.text: At 4,000 residents it is 80 each, and if the village shrinks the fixed part per person rises.
It cannot be derived, because the account does not separate the reservoir charge.
options.misconception: says the total cost is unusable without a component breakdown

options.text: It is 4,000 each, because the reservoir serves exactly that many residents.
options.misconception: reverses the numerator and denominator in a per-person division

questions.explanation: The total annual cost over 4,000 residents is 320,000 over 4,000, which is 80 per person. Because part of that cost is fixed, losing residents raises the charge each remaining resident faces.
questions.hint: Spread the total cost over the residents served.
